semantic_core.text: The PLC output triac U14 had an open anode due to a hairline solder fracture under its package.
Contributing: the cabinet intake filter was 90% clogged, lowering airflow and raising the component temperature to 75°C.
Contributing: solar radiation and heat from nearby transformer T-1 kept the cabinet interior above 60°C.
A calibrated probe showed the 70.1°C oil setpoint was correct; no sensor error contributed to the failure.
At 10:30, the outdoor heat wave at Synthetic Substation North caused the transformer load to rise to 37.6 MVA for more than two hours.
At 11:45:00, the top-oil temperature reached 70.1°C, which crossed the automatic fan-start setpoint.
At 11:45:02, the controller energized the stage-one fan bank by closing channel 14 for two seconds.
At 11:45:09, fan phase currents remained zero, so the controller's warning timer did not even start.
At 11:55, oil temperature climbed to 77.3°C, so the controller sent a stage-two command on the same channel.
At 12:20, the hot-oil alarm appeared; the operator remotely reissued the start command from the HMI.
The remote reissue produced no fan activity because the same triac had no gate path.
At 12:32, the winding-temperature function reached 100°C and tripped breaker 52T after its two-second delay.
At 12:32:02, breaker 52T opened, isolating T-2 and its 22 MW load, though the station bus stayed supplied by T-1.
Oil samples at 14:00 contained 0.24 mg/L furan, up from 0.03 mg/L in the 2025 annual test.
The dissolved gas sample taken the next day found ethylene at 142 ppm, versus a 2025 baseline of 15 ppm, confirming a thermal fault.
T-2 remained unavailable for 11 hours; no customer demand was shed because the export line had headroom.
Technicians replaced the failed triac with an industrial-grade module and installed a redundant cooling power path.
A filter-clogging differential pressure switch now alarms at 75%, and the filter is cleaned monthly.
Engineering added a hard-wired manual start button at the local panel to start fans independent of the PLC output.
A predetermined spring-time load cap of 34 MVA on T-2 protects it until the cooling cabinet upgrades are complete.

semantic_core.text: An errant 0.85 multiplier in the cooling control algorithm reduced the apparent oil-temperature input.
That constant had been written during a firmware update thirty days earlier and never cross-checked.
The 198 MVA load flow exceeded the transformer's 150 MVA self-cooling rating, so fans were mandatory.
A direct measurement with a test rig confirmed the RTD was accurate; no sensor fault existed.
At 13:10, the outdoor heat wave caused the real top-oil temperature to exceed 82°C.
The control system, however, calculated a top-oil value of 69.7°C at that same moment.
At 13:15, when the actual top-oil reached 88.2°C, the calculated value finally reached 75.0°C.
The controller then commanded stage-one fans to start, which they did at 13:16.
By 13:18, the transformer's oil temperature continued upward to 91°C because fan airflow needs time.
At 13:20, the high-oil-temperature alarm activated in the control room at exactly 90.0°C.
The fan inductor current and airflow increased, but the winding temperature kept climbing to 103°C.
At 13:22, the winding-temperature relay tripped the generator breaker after a five-second deliberation.
Breaker 86G opened at 13:22:05, separating the generator unit from the grid and losing 178 MW of real power.
An oil sample taken after the trip gave acetylene 23 ppm, thus indicating an incipient thermal fault.
The transformer remained out for nine hours; during that time the plant operated at reduced output.
Winding resistance measurements showed a four percent increase in the low-voltage phase A, suggesting local annealing.
The controller's scaling constant was corrected to 1.00 and a firmware checksum check was installed.
All cooling-control software parameter changes now require a second-person verification before upload.
The new high-temperature fan start setpoint was lowered to 70°C to provide earlier cooling action.
A temporary operating guide caps the generator at 120 MVA until the transformer inspection and diagnostics are completed.
